patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of vertigo, progressive fatigue, and intermittent tingling in the hands over the past 8 months, previously attributed to anxiety and migraine
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Kowalski is a 31-year-old right-handed graduate student who was admitted for further evaluation of an 8-month history of episodic vertigo, progressive fatigue, and intermittent paresthesias that have been attributed to anxiety and migraine by her primary care physician and a prior neurologist. The patient reports that her symptoms began approximately 8 months ago when she developed sudden-onset room-spinning vertigo that lasted about 3 days and then gradually resolved over a week. She was seen in the emergency department at that time, diagnosed with a recurrence of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo despite the Dix-Hallpike test being equivocal, and was discharged with meclizine. She saw her primary care physician in follow-up who noted she appeared anxious and attributed residual lightheadedness to her generalized anxiety disorder.

Approximately 4 months ago, she developed tingling and numbness in the fingertips of both hands that she noticed primarily in the morning and which would come and go throughout the day. She was evaluated by her primary care physician who checked basic blood work including a CBC and metabolic panel, both of which were normal, and told her the symptoms were likely related to anxiety or possibly carpal tunnel syndrome from long hours typing her thesis. She was given wrist splints which she wore intermittently without clear benefit.

Over the past 2 months, she has noticed a profound and worsening fatigue unlike anything she has experienced before. She describes it as an overwhelming sense of exhaustion that is not proportional to her activity level and is not relieved by sleep. She sleeps 9 to 10 hours per night but wakes feeling unrefreshed. Her academic performance has suffered significantly. She has also noticed that her symptoms, particularly the tingling and a vague sense of imbalance, seem to worsen noticeably after hot showers, which she has attributed to orthostatic hypotension or deconditioning.

Three weeks ago, she experienced a second distinct episode of vertigo lasting approximately 2 days, associated with nausea and mild gait unsteadiness. Her roommate noticed that she seemed to have difficulty walking in a straight line during this episode. She was seen by a neurologist who ordered a brain MRI which showed a few scattered non-specific white matter lesions. The neurologist told her these were likely related to migraine and anxiety, noting that white matter changes can be seen in young women with migraine. However, her primary care physician was not entirely reassured and referred her for inpatient evaluation to a tertiary center for a second opinion.

The patient herself is skeptical that anything serious is going on and has been told by multiple providers that her symptoms are anxiety-related. She admits that the escalating symptoms have increased her anxiety, creating what she perceives as a vicious cycle.

results.title: Oligoclonal band negative multiple sclerosis: clinical and demographic features, disease course, and prognosis
results.summary: Approximately 5-10% of patients with clinically definite MS have persistently negative oligoclonal bands. These patients may have a milder disease course and are more likely to have primary progressive MS.

results.title: The 2017 McDonald Criteria for the Diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis
results.summary: CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time in the 2017 McDonald criteria, but their absence does not exclude the diagnosis if DIT is demonstrated by other means such as new lesions on follow-up MRI.

results.title: CSF findings in patients with MS and negative OCB
results.summary: OCB-negative MS patients tend to present with milder CSF inflammatory profiles and may require more rigorous MRI follow-up to establish dissemination in time for diagnosis.

output.summary: Oligoclonal bands are absent in approximately 5-10% of confirmed MS cases. The 2017 McDonald criteria do not require positive OCB for diagnosis if dissemination in space and time can be demonstrated by MRI criteria alone. OCB-negative MS may be associated with a milder phenotype. Diagnosis should not be excluded solely on the basis of negative OCB.

differential.key_features: AQP4-IgG positivity, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (≥3 vertebral segments), severe or bilateral optic neuritis, and area postrema syndrome — must be excluded before committing to MS
MOG-IgG positivity (cell-based assay), often bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis, ADEM-like presentations in younger patients, frequent lesion resolution on follow-up MRI
Leptomeningeal/pachymeningeal enhancement, hypothalamic-pituitary involvement, cranial neuropathies, hilar adenopathy on imaging, elevated serum/CSF ACE, lymphopenia
Elevated ESR/CRP, multifocal infarcts crossing vascular territories, vessel-wall enhancement on high-resolution MRA, systemic features (rash, arthritis, renal involvement)
Encephalopathy + branch retinal artery occlusion + sensorineural hearing loss; corpus callosum 'snowball' lesions characteristic
Monophasic course, post-infectious/post-vaccination trigger, encephalopathy hallmark, large confluent lesions that often resolve

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis — findings are non-specific and do not contribute to dissemination in space or time.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for visualising demyelinating plaques; ordering CT delays diagnosis and adds radiation without clinical benefit.
No cardiac indication in a typical MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod initiation (bradyarrhythmia risk) — not as part of MS diagnostic workup.
FDG-PET is not indicated for MS diagnosis or DMT decisions; it does not differentiate demyelination from mimics and adds substantial cost.

sequence_constraints.reason: Standard pre-LP imaging: confirm absence of mass effect / herniation risk on brain MRI before lumbar puncture

critical_actions: Establish dissemination in space (DIS) using brain and spinal-cord MRI in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord)
Establish dissemination in time (DIT) by demonstrating simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, a new lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (per McDonald 2017)
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before committing to an MS diagnosis and DMT
Order CSF analysis with paired serum to assess oligoclonal bands and IgG index
Treat the acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3–5 days), with plasma exchange reserved for steroid-refractory severe relapses
Initiate a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) after relapse stabilization; choice between platform vs. high-efficacy agent based on disease activity, MRI burden, and patient preference
Check JC virus antibody serostatus before considering natalizumab; verify up-to-date vaccinations (especially live-attenuated) before initiating B-cell depleting or S1P-modulator DMTs
Counsel on Uhthoff phenomenon, heat avoidance, smoking cessation, and vitamin D supplementation as modifiable lifestyle factors
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting McDonald 2017 criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start natalizumab in a JC virus-antibody-positive patient (especially with high index) without explicit benefit-risk discussion of PML
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring; avoid in patients with second-degree AV block, prior MI, or severe sleep apnea
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as a maintenance treatment for MS — they are ineffective long-term and carry significant harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal-cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS criteria — cord lesions change relapse counting and management
key_reasoning_points: MS is a clinical-radiographic diagnosis: McDonald 2017 requires dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) plus exclusion of better explanations — no single test confirms it

MS-typical MRI regions are periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord — recognising a lesion in three of these regions establishes DIS for an attack-meeting clinical event
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2 bands not present in paired serum) can substitute for DIT under McDonald 2017 when DIS is met — this changes the calculus for clinically isolated syndromes

Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies), peripheral, dorsolateral or dorsal-column spinal cord lesions strongly favour MS over NMOSD (which characteristically produces longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)
Open-ring enhancement with the opening oriented toward the cortex is a high-specificity sign of demyelination, distinguishing tumefactive MS from neoplasm and abscess
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be ordered as cell-based assays, not ELISA — the older ELISA-based AQP4 assays have unacceptable false-negative rates
T1 hypointense 'black holes' indicate axonal loss from prior inflammatory episodes and contribute evidence of dissemination in time even without simultaneous enhancing lesions

Choice of DMT — platform agent (interferon-β, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) vs. high-efficacy agent (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine, S1P modulators) — should weigh disease activity, MRI burden, patient comorbidities, JCV serostatus, and reproductive plans
If the initial brain MRI does not include the spinal cord, extending imaging to cervical and thoracic cord is essential — both for diagnostic DIS and for relapse counting

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

metadata.key_diagnostic_challenge: OCB-negative MS with non-specific initial MRI resembling migraine-related white matter changes; diagnosis requires persistent clinical suspicion, multimodal paraclinical testing, and follow-up imaging to demonstrate dissemination in time
metadata.teaching_points: Not all MS presents with classic findings. Negative OCB, atypical MRI, and normal neurological exam can occur. Uhthoff phenomenon and episodic neurological symptoms disseminated in time and space should raise suspicion even when initial workup is equivocal.
metadata.revision_reason: per-case audit: the action named these mimic-exclusion assays and its expected_finding reported them negative, but the laboratory payload contained none of them — AQP4_IgG, HIV
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Non-classic brain MRI (few subcortical lesions, no Dawson fingers, no enhancement) plus non-specific clinical features means McDonald 2017 DIS/DIT criteria cannot be met from initial workup alone — requires spine MRI, OCT/VEP, and follow-up MRI to establish diagnosis or to retain CIS
